/-!
# Erdős Problem 370

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/370](https://www.erdosproblems.com/370)
-/

namespace Erdos370

/--
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the largest prime factor of $n$ is $< n^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and
the largest prime factor of $n + 1$ is $< (n + 1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Steinerberger has pointed out this problem has a trivial solution.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos370.lean",
formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/XC0R/formal-conjectures/blob/f58dea7d2cc5c9da2e050ec80a73e838b54a6dd2/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/370.lean#L73"]
theorem erdos_370 : answer(True) ↔
    { n | Nat.maxPrimeFac n < √n ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) < √(n + 1) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos370

reformulations.difference: Lean ranges over all natural numbers and uses a total largest-prime-factor function, whereas the source’s largest-prime-factor terminology is ordinarily meaningful for integers greater than 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Nat.maxPrimeFac 0 = 0 and Nat.maxPrimeFac 1 = 1, so the first strict inequality fails at both 0 and 1. Consequently every member of the Lean set already satisfies n > 1, and adding that restriction leaves the set unchanged. For n > 1, Nat.maxPrimeFac is indeed the largest prime divisor. The domain-restriction equivalence and prime-divisor characterization were proved in the scratch file without sorry.

sources_consulted: https://www.erdosproblems.com/370 — retrieved through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.erdosproblems.com/370, with formulas recovered from the rendered HTML’s MathJax attributes.
